notes: PDCI-RDA is the ruling slot 0 (Houphouët-Boigny's pro-French single party) instead of MD's slot 18; slot 13 holds the party-state apparatus around Philippe Yacé as coalition partner. MD 2000 parties (RDR, PIT, FPI, RHDP, MPCI) are anachronistic and replaced. Sanwi separatists sit in slot 23 as the Kingdom of Sanwi.

0.name: Parti démocratique de Côte d'Ivoire – Rassemblement démocratique africain
0.english: Democratic Party of Ivory Coast – African Democratic Rally
0.native_full: Parti démocratique de Côte d'Ivoire – Rassemblement démocratique africain
0.text:
The PDCI-RDA grew out of the planters' movement Félix Houphouët-Boigny led against forced labour in the 1940s and became the Ivorian section of the African Democratic Rally. Since independence in 1960 it has been the sole legal party, and on 1 January 1970 it rules unchallenged under President Houphouët-Boigny, with Philippe Yacé as secretary-general.

The party fuses cocoa and coffee wealth, French partnership and patronage into a single machine. It defends open markets, foreign investment and close ties to Paris, opposes Soviet influence across West Africa and backs Biafra against Lagos. Its leverage lies in the Baoulé heartland, the planter class and control of every post in the state.
0.wiki: Democratic Party of Côte d'Ivoire – African Democratic Rally

1.name: Archidiocèse d'Abidjan
1.text:
The Catholic Church is the most organised body in Ivory Coast outside the ruling party. Its mission schools trained much of the southern elite, and since 1960 Archbishop Bernard Yago, the first Ivorian to head the see of Abidjan, has led it as a respected national voice.

The Church preaches social peace, family and education, cooperates closely with the government and treats atheistic communism as a threat. It speaks for Catholic civil servants, teachers and the urban middle class of the lagoon region. Its leverage lies in its school network and its moral authority, which can make it a moderate conservative pole if the single party ever opens up.

2.name: Jeunesse du Rassemblement démocratique africain de Côte d'Ivoire
2.english: Youth of the African Democratic Rally of Ivory Coast
2.native_full: Jeunesse du Rassemblement démocratique africain de Côte d'Ivoire
2.text:
The JRDACI was founded in 1959 as the youth wing of the ruling party and drew in the first generation of university-trained cadres. Several of its leaders fell foul of the regime during the alleged plots of 1963, and in 1970 it survives as a supervised forum for young graduates waiting for promotion.

Its members want faster Ivorianisation of senior posts, more say for younger officials and gradual liberalisation of the single-party system, while sharing the regime's pro-Western economic course. Its base is the educated youth of Abidjan and Bouaké. Its leverage is generational: the state cannot run without the graduates it speaks for.

3.name: Union générale des travailleurs de Côte d'Ivoire
3.english: General Union of Workers of Ivory Coast
3.native_full: Union générale des travailleurs de Côte d'Ivoire
3.text:
The UGTCI was created in 1962 to bring the country's trade unions under one roof, closely tied to the PDCI-RDA. Led by Joseph Coffie, it is the only legal labour centre on 1 January 1970 and practises what the regime calls responsible participation rather than open confrontation.

The union seeks wage increases, social security and Ivorianisation of skilled jobs held by expatriates, but rejects class struggle and Marxist unions. Its members are dockers, railwaymen, civil servants and factory workers in Abidjan. Its leverage lies in the port and the railway to Upper Volta, whose stoppage would choke the export economy.
3.wiki: General Union of Workers of Côte d'Ivoire

4.name: Les Rouges de la FEANF
4.text:
Ivorian students in France form one of the most radical sections of the Federation of Black African Students in France, the FEANF. Their pro-Soviet core reads Lenin in the Latin Quarter, maintains contacts with the French Communist Party and denounces Houphouët-Boigny as the chief agent of French neo-colonialism.

They call for nationalisation of plantations and foreign firms, alignment with the socialist camp and an end to French military bases. Their base is tiny at home but influential among future teachers, doctors and engineers. Their leverage lies in the moment they return, carrying ideas the single party cannot easily absorb.

5.name: Union nationale des étudiants de Côte d'Ivoire
5.english: National Union of Students of Ivory Coast
5.native_full: Union nationale des étudiants de Côte d'Ivoire
5.text:
UNECI organised the students of the young University of Abidjan and grew steadily more defiant of the regime. In May 1969 it led a strike that ended with police occupying the campus and students detained. The government dissolved it and set up the loyal MEECI in its place, so on 1 January 1970 UNECI is banned and works underground.

Its activists combine anti-imperialism, New Left slogans and demands for campus autonomy, and they attack French control of the economy. Their base is students and young secondary teachers. Their leverage is disruption: strikes and protests in Abidjan that embarrass a regime proud of its stability.

6.name: Les Éburnéens
6.text:
In the Bété country around Gagnoa, resentment at Baoulé dominance, land sales to migrants and the PDCI monopoly has found a voice in Kragbé Gnagbé, a young Bété intellectual who dreams of a separate Eburnean republic and wants to register an opposition nationalist party.

The Eburneans reject the French-guided order of Abidjan, demand that land stay with indigenous communities and view northern and foreign planters as intruders. Their base is Bété villagers in the cocoa belt of the west-centre. Their leverage is local and volatile: an uprising in the Gagnoa region could force the regime into a costly crackdown.

7.name: Les Amis de Conakry
7.text:
Ahmed Sékou Touré's Guinea, which broke with France in 1958, is Houphouët-Boigny's ideological rival next door. A scattering of Ivorian exiles, northern traders and radical officials admire Conakry's single-party revolution and keep quiet contact with Guinean emissaries and the émigré networks around Kwame Nkrumah.

They favour a disciplined vanguard state, a break with Paris, nationalisation of the export trade and alignment with the anti-imperialist camp. Their base is small and clandestine, strongest among Malinké traders and disaffected cadres. Their leverage would come from Guinean backing and from any crisis that discredits the French alliance.

8.name: Husayniyya de Treichville
8.text:
The Lebanese community of Abidjan, largely Shia families from southern Lebanon, dominates retail and wholesale trade in Treichville and the Plateau. Its prayer halls follow events at home closely, especially the work of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who toured West Africa in 1967 and founded the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut in 1969.

The community favours a modern, socially engaged Shia identity, education and charitable networks, and keeps clear of Ivorian politics in exchange for security. Its base is merchants and shopkeepers. Its leverage lies in credit and commerce: much of the country's distribution trade passes through Lebanese hands.

9.name: Les Fidèles de Najaf
9.text:
A handful of Lebanese families in Abidjan send their sons to study in the seminaries of Najaf, and a few returning students preach a stricter, clerical Shi'ism than the community's businessmen practise. They meet in private homes during Muharram and follow the senior marjas of Iraq.

They want religious life organised under clerical guidance, strict observance and solidarity with the Shia struggle in Lebanon and Iraq, and distrust both the secular West and the Soviet bloc. Their base is very small. Their leverage lies in religious legitimacy, which grows whenever Middle Eastern crises reach the diaspora.

10.name: Tijāniyya
10.text:
The Tijaniyya brotherhood is the leading Sufi order among the Muslims of northern Ivory Coast and the Dioula trading diaspora in the south. Its imams and marabouts in Kong, Bondoukou, Odienné and Treichville work comfortably with the PDCI-RDA, which courts them as intermediaries to the Muslim north.

The order preaches obedience to legitimate authority, piety and Qur'anic education, and rejects both radical reformism and political Islam. Its followers are traders, transporters and northern farmers. Its leverage lies in the networks of zawiyas and Qur'anic schools that link the northern savanna to the markets of Abidjan.

11.name: Les Héritiers de Samory
11.text:
Samory Touré's Wassoulou state carved an Islamic empire across the northern savanna in the 1880s and 1890s, burning Kong and resisting the French until 1898. Among a few young Qur'anic scholars in the north, his memory is now recast as a model of armed Islamic rule against unbelieving power.

They reject the secular republic, its French patrons and the accommodating brotherhoods alike, and dream of a state governed by sharia. Their following is tiny and scattered in Odienné, Touba and Korhogo. Their leverage would come only from northern grievances and from radical teachers arriving from abroad.

12.name: Union culturelle musulmane
12.text:
The Muslim Cultural Union was founded in Dakar in 1953 by reform-minded scholars returning from Al-Azhar and the Hejaz, and quickly spread to Bamako, Bouaké and Abidjan. Its Ivorian circles, linked to the Wahhabi-leaning traders of the Dioula community, operate on 1 January 1970 under close police watch.

The UCM calls for modern Arabic-language schools, a purified Islam free of maraboutic practices and a stronger Muslim voice in public life. Its base is merchants, teachers and young northerners in the towns. Its leverage lies in its schools and in Gulf and Egyptian links that fund mosques and scholarships.

13.name: Les Barons du Parti
13.text:
Behind Houphouët-Boigny stand the barons of the party-state: Philippe Yacé, secretary-general of the PDCI-RDA and president of the National Assembly, the regional secretaries and the ministers who run the administration. Yacé is widely seen as the president's dauphin.

The barons care less for doctrine than for order, continuity and the single-party monopoly. They balance French advisers and Ivorian cadres, ethnic quotas and regional patronage, and avoid entanglement in the East-West quarrel beyond what the president dictates. Their base is the party apparatus and the civil service. Their leverage is the machine itself, which will decide the succession.

14.name: Les Chefs de Canton
14.text:
The canton and village chiefs created by French administration still mediate between the state and rural Ivory Coast. Akan kings and chiefs of the Agni, Abron and Baoulé, Senufo elders in the north and lineage heads in the west settle land disputes and deliver votes for the single party.

They defend customary land rights, respect for elders and the authority of the chieftaincy against young cadres and migrants alike. They have little interest in the Cold War and much in local power. Their leverage lies in land: every plantation in the cocoa belt depends on the goodwill of those who allocate it.

15.name: Chambre de commerce de Côte d'Ivoire
15.english: Chamber of Commerce of Ivory Coast
15.native_full: Chambre de commerce de Côte d'Ivoire
15.text:
The Chamber of Commerce gathers the French trading houses, banks, timber firms and industrialists who dominate the modern economy of Abidjan, along with a rising circle of Ivorian business owners. Houses such as CFAO and SCOA remain central to import and export trade on 1 January 1970.

The Chamber defends the investment code, the CFA franc and its link to the French treasury, low taxes and free transfer of profits. It is staunchly anti-communist and close to the French embassy. Its leverage lies in capital: the much-praised Ivorian miracle depends on foreign money that can leave as quickly as it came.

16.name: Le Miracle ivoirien
16.text:
Around Henri Konan Bédié, Minister of Economy and Finance since 1966, a group of young technocrats champions the liberal growth model that has given Ivory Coast some of the fastest growth in Africa. They prize open markets, foreign capital and export agriculture over planning and state ownership.

They want lower barriers to trade, a stable CFA franc, private Ivorian entrepreneurs and gradual replacement of expatriates by trained nationals, while keeping firmly in the Western camp. Their base is the ministries, the banks and Ivorian businessmen. Their leverage lies in the growth figures that make Abidjan the showcase of capitalist Africa.

17.name: Les Gardiens du Banco
17.text:
Foresters, scientists at the research stations around Adiopodoumé and a few teachers in Abidjan watch with alarm as timber exports and new plantations devour the southern rainforest. They rally around the Banco forest reserve on the edge of the capital as a symbol of what remains.

They call for protected reserves, controlled logging and replanting, and warn that the cocoa boom is consuming the land it depends on. Their base is a small circle of experts and civil servants. Their leverage lies in science and in the fact that timber is the country's next export after coffee and cocoa.

18.name: Les Rescapés d'Assabou
18.text:
The alleged plots of 1963 and 1964 sent dozens of PDCI-RDA cadres to the Assabou prison near Yamoussoukro. Among them was Jean-Baptiste Mockey, once the party's radical organiser, freed in 1967 and slowly rehabilitated. The survivors remain a discreet current of the old RDA left.

They favour a more egalitarian path: state-led development, cooperatives for small planters, a stronger say for workers and distance from the French embrace, without breaking with the party. Their base is older militants of the 1940s struggle. Their leverage lies in memory and legitimacy within the party that once jailed them.

19.name: Les Maoïstes de Cocody
19.text:
At the University of Abidjan in Cocody and among students returning from Paris, the Chinese Cultural Revolution has won small reading circles that treat the Little Red Book as a guide for Africa. They split from pro-Soviet comrades and see Moscow as revisionist.

They preach a peasant revolution based in the countryside, self-reliance and a break with both superpowers and with France. Their base is students and a few young teachers. Their leverage is limited to campus agitation, but their writing reaches workers and secondary schools and keeps the security services busy.

20.name: Ligue des originaires de Côte d'Ivoire
20.english: League of Natives of Ivory Coast
20.native_full: Ligue des originaires de Côte d'Ivoire
20.text:
The LOCI emerged in 1958 among unemployed Abidjan youths who blamed Dahomeyan and Togolese clerks for taking their jobs, and its campaign ended in violent attacks on foreigners. Its networks survive among urban job seekers and petty traders who resent the many African immigrants the regime welcomes.

The League demands jobs and trading licences reserved for Ivorians, limits on immigration from neighbouring states and the removal of expatriates from the civil service. Its base is the urban poor of Treichville and Adjamé. Its leverage lies in street mobilisation whenever unemployment rises.

21.name: Les Anciens de l'OAS
21.text:
After the Algerian war, a number of French settlers, mercenaries and former soldiers sympathetic to the OAS found work in the security firms, plantations and bars of Abidjan. They keep in touch with mercenary circles that have fought in the Congo and look on Biafra as the next frontier.

They despise decolonisation, admire authoritarian strongmen and offer their services against any communist threat. Their numbers are small and their base lies among expatriate security men and ex-soldiers. Their leverage lies in weapons, connections with French intelligence and willingness to fight for hire.

22.name: Forces armées nationales de Côte d'Ivoire
22.native_full: Forces armées nationales de Côte d'Ivoire
22.text:
The Ivorian army is small, deliberately kept weak by a president who trusts the French 43rd Marine Infantry Battalion at Port-Bouët more than his own officers. Its chief of staff, General Thomas d'Aquin Ouattara, commands a few thousand men and a gendarmerie under close political supervision.

The officers share the regime's pro-Western stance but resent their modest budgets and the French presence. Their base is the barracks of Abidjan, Bouaké and Daloa. Their leverage is the threat that haunts every West African capital since the coups in Ghana, Togo and Mali: the army could act alone.

23.name: Royaume du Sanwi
23.text:
The Agni Kingdom of Sanwi, with its royal court at Krinjabo near Aboisso, claims a separate protectorate treaty with France from 1843. In 1959 its king proclaimed secession and was crushed, and the Sanwi question revived in 1969 with new arrests. On 1 January 1970 its separatists are suppressed but defiant.

The Sanwi movement demands recognition of the kingdom's treaty rights, autonomy or independence and the restoration of royal authority in the south-east. Its base is Agni villagers and notables. Its leverage lies in legitimacy rooted in history and in the risk of unrest on the border with Ghana.
